newsitem.title: NIGERIA: African first ladies talk peace as war continues.
newsitem.headline: African first ladies talk peace as war continues.

text.p: More than a dozen wives of African leaders assembled in the Nigerian capital on Monday against the backdrop of civil war in Zaire to discuss how they can use their influence to bring peace to the world's poorest continent.

"We must use this summit to show our usefulness in the peaceful resolution of conflicts," Nigerian first lady Maryam Abacha, initiator of the conference, told her counterparts who had already arrived for a reception on Sunday.

Dubbed "The first summit of African first ladies on peace," it was to be declared open around noon (1100 GMT) by Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha in the capital's imposing International Conference Centre.

"This summit is not going to be just a talkshop but a forum that will proffer permanent solutions to the myriad of socio-political problems facing the continent," the spokesman of Abacha's wife, Mamman Nassir, told reporters.
Africa's latest war is in Zaire where veteran strongman Mobutu Sese Seko looks about to lose his 32-year-old grip on power to Laurent Kabila's rebels.
The rebels said after failed peace talks on Sunday they would push on toward Zaire's capital Kinshaha while ailing Mobutu considers Kabila's demand for his immediate resignation.
Like most wars in Africa, the suffering is greatest for refugees, 91 of whom were killed in a stampede on a train in rebel-held northeast Zaire on Sunday.

The Abuja conference is being staged with backing from Nigeria's military government and according to foreign minister Tom Ikimi: "The major objective of the summit is to find ways women can be involved in conflict resolution in Africa."
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation with 100 million people, has itself been in crisis since 1993 when the army annulled a presidential election that would have ushered in democracy.
The Abacha government is shunned by Western nations and countries like South Africa over its slow pace of democratisation and alleged human rights violations.

It is not certain if South Africa would be represented but first ladies who arrived in Abuja on Sunday included those of Namibia, Angola, Niger, Sierra Leone, Senegal, Gabon, Burundi, Equitorial Guinea, Gambia, Guinea, Chad and Zambia. Others are Guinea Bissau, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Burkina Faso, Tanzania and the interim head of state of war-ravaged Liberia, Ruth Perry.

Organisation of African Unity (OAU) secretary-general Salim Ahmed Salim arrived in Nigeria last Thursday for the conference while a representative of United Nations secretary-general Koffi Annan was expected.
Mrs Abacha, a 50-year-old mother of 11 children, said the summit was a result of the Beijing conference on Women of 1995. The Abuja conference ends on Wednesday.
